newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba sticks to growth target despite hurricane.
newsitem.headline: Cuba sticks to growth target despite hurricane.

text.p: The Cuban government said Thursday it would reach its five percent target for economic growth this year despite damage caused by Hurricane Lili.

Vice President Carlos Lage, seeking to allay fears the island nation was crippled by the storm, told the ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma that the damage, while serious, would not stop Cuba's economic recovery.

"We can assure you that the proposal of finishing the year with growth of five percent will be surpassed, and that growth will continue in 1997," said Lage, who is viewed as the architect of Cuba's economic reform process.
Hurricane Lili ripped through central and western areas of Cuba last Thursday and Friday, damaging crops, destroying more than 5,000 homes and cutting power lines and communications.
The storm came a blow at a time when Cuba is slowly emerging from a five-year economic crisis caused by the collapse of the former Soviet Union, its longtime economic benefactor and trade partner.
Lage, who is scheduled to travel to Canada this weekend, said Cuba was also facing the effects of the seven-month-old Helms-Burton law.
The recently enacted U.S. legislation tightens Washington's 34-year economic embargo against the island by seeking to discourage foreign investment.
"Neither Lili, nor Helms-Burton can stop the recovery of the Cuban economy," he said.

Lage said that storm damage was "of large proportions," but there was still no overall figure for damage to the economy. He noted in particular damage to food crops, citrus plantations -- a large part of which are used for export products -- and sugar cane plantations.

Officials said earlier this week that most crops in eight of the country's 14 provinces were affected by the storm. Some 670,000 hectares (1.66 million acres) of sugar cane were affected, just months ahead of the 1996-97 sugar harvest. But the sugar ministry has said although cane was flattened or flooded, much of it will be useable for the harvest.
"These plantations may have reduced yields but they are not lost," Lage said, adding it was still possible to continue improving Cuba's sugar production.

Before the hurricane, sugar experts said Cuba could produce around 5.2 million to 5.3 million tonnes of sugar, up from 4.45 million tonnes in the 1995-96 harvest. Government officials had not given a target but had said the aim was to improve on 4.45 million tonnes.

Lage said the storm swept some 154,000 tonnes of citrus fruit to the ground, a third of the production targeted for the year. Some 26,800 hectares (66,200 acres) of bananas were damaged, as well as 9,700 hectares (23,900 acres) of rice and 8,040 hectares (19,900 acres) of beans, root vegetables and other food crops. This was bound to put an additional burden on the state to find cash for imports, Lage said.
He said Cuba's creditors need not worry they would not be paid. "Cuba will fulfill all its financial obligations," he said in response to a question.
